title: GATE CS 2010
instructions: Verified source header: 2010, CS: Computer Science and Information Technology. Single paper; no set/session designation. The exact selected 24-page scan and physical filename 2010.pdf are preserved. The end marker is on page 16; pages 17-24 are rough-work leaves.

Source page 1 specifies 65 objective questions, 100 marks and three hours. Q1-25 are one mark; Q26-55 two marks; General Aptitude Q56-60 one mark and Q61-65 two marks. Ten aptitude questions carry 15 marks. Attempt all; no section choices or descriptive questions.

Original order is retained in five navigation blocks: one-mark Q1-25, two-mark Q26-47, common-data Q48-51 (two pairs), linked answers Q52-55 (two pairs), General Aptitude Q56-65. Each MCQ permits one selected option.
Documented negative marking, source page 1: wrong Q1-25 and Q56-60 lose 1/3 mark; wrong Q26-52, Q54 and Q61-65 lose 2/3 mark. Q53 and Q55 have no penalty. Unattempted questions earn zero.

Documented linked-credit rule, source page 1: Q53 is evaluated only if Q52 is correctly answered; Q55 only if Q54 is correctly answered. A wrong or blank first answer makes the second ineligible for credit. The server enforces both the prerequisite and zero second-question penalty.

Every question has an independently authored worked reference, not an authenticated official key. Provenance distinguishes visually checked Made Easy key entries, individually reviewed GATE Overflow discussions and cache-only question links. Direct automated discussion downloads returned HTTP 403; accessible web discussions were used for targeted checks.

Disputed Q34, Q48, Q49 and Q63 (8 marks) are retained literally and require labeled post-submission self-assessment. Q34 has a conflicting printed Made Easy key; Q48-49 depend on cache timing assumptions; Q63 has competing reading interpretations. Conventional reference choices are not definite automatic grades.

Independent question IDs, keys, diagram assets and original-record provenance isolate this paper from book records and book-based mocks. Timer, calculator, palette, autosave, refresh/resume and automatic submission use the existing test environment.

questions.text: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph. Define $\xi(G)=\sum_d i_d\times d$, where $i_d$ is the number of vertices of degree $d$ in $G$. If $S$ and $T$ are two different trees with $\xi(S)=\xi(T)$, then
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: The handshaking lemma gives $\xi(G)=2|E|$. A tree with $v$ vertices has $v-1$ edges. Equal degree sums therefore imply equal numbers of vertices: $|S|=|T|$.

questions.text: Newton-Raphson method is used to compute a root of the equation $x^2-13=0$ with 3.5 as the initial value. The approximation after one iteration is
What is the possible number of reflexive relations on a set of 5 elements?
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: There are 25 ordered pairs. Reflexivity fixes the five diagonal pairs; each of the remaining 20 pairs may independently be included or excluded. Hence $2^{20}$.

questions.text: Consider the set S = {1, $\omega$, $\omega^2$}, where $\omega$ and $\omega^2$ are cube roots of unity. If $*$ denotes the multiplication operation, the structure {S, *} forms
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Multiplication is closed and associative on the three cube roots, 1 is the identity, and $\omega$ and $\omega^2$ are inverses. This is a cyclic group of order 3. A ring or field would also require a specified addition operation.

questions.text: What is the value of $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\dfrac1n\right)^{2n}$?
questions.subject: 11. Engg. Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: The logarithm of the expression is $2n\log(1-1/n)\to-2$, so the limit is $e^{-2}$.

questions.subject: 4. COA

questions.text: In a binary tree with n nodes, every node has an odd number of descendants. Every node is considered to be its own descendant. What is the number of nodes in the tree that have exactly one child?
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: If a node had exactly one child, its subtree size would be one plus that child's odd subtree size, hence even. This contradicts the stated odd descendant count at every node. Thus no node has exactly one child.

questions.text: Two alternative packages A and B are available for processing a database having $10^k$ records. Package A requires $0.0001n^2$ time units and package B requires $10n\log_{10}n$ time units to process $n$ records. What is the smallest value of $k$ for which package B will be preferred over A?
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms

questions.text: Consider a $B^+$ tree in which the maximum number of keys in a node is 5. What is the minimum number of keys in any non-root node?
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: A maximum of five keys means at most six child pointers in an internal node. A non-root internal node needs at least $\lceil6/2\rceil=3$ children and therefore two separator keys. Leaf minimum occupancy can differ; the question asks the minimum in any non-root node, so 2 is attainable internally.

questions.text:
Which of the following concurrency control protocols ensure both conflict serializability and freedom from deadlock?
I.  2-phase locking
II.  Time-stamp ordering
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: Two-phase locking guarantees conflict serializability but may deadlock. Timestamp ordering orders conflicting operations by timestamps and aborts/restarts transactions rather than forming a lock-wait cycle, giving both requested properties.

questions.text: A system uses FIFO policy for page replacement. It has 4 page frames with no pages loaded to begin with. The system first accesses 100 distinct pages in some order and then accesses the same 100 pages but now in the reverse order. How many page faults will occur?
questions.subject: 5. Operating Systems
questions.referenceAnswer: The first 100 distinct accesses all fault. The reverse pass first hits the four pages still resident and then faults on the remaining 96 pages. Total: 100+96=196. A direct FIFO simulation gives the same count.

questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true?
I. Shortest remaining time first scheduling may cause starvation.
II. Preemptive scheduling may cause starvation.
III. Round robin is better than FCFS in terms of response time.
questions.rawTopic: Process Management-I (Introduction, Process, Threads & CPU Scheduling)
questions.subject: 5. Operating Systems
questions.referenceAnswer: An indefinite stream of short jobs can starve a long job under shortest-remaining-time scheduling. Preemptive priority scheduling can also starve low-priority jobs, so II says may, not must. Round robin offers an early time slice to waiting jobs rather than waiting for an entire long FCFS predecessor; III uses the conventional interactive-response-time comparison. Thus the intended statements are I, II and III.

notes: Answer transcribed from the printed chapter key, PDF page 5 / book page 533.

questions.text: Consider a company that assembles computers. The probability of a faulty assembly of any computer is $p$. The company therefore subjects each computer to a testing process. This testing process gives the correct result for any computer with a probability of $q$. What is the probability of a computer being declared faulty?
questions.subject: 11. Engg. Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: Partition into truly faulty and truly good computers. A faulty one is declared faulty with probability pq; a good one is incorrectly declared faulty with probability $(1-p)(1-q)$. Add the disjoint cases: $pq+(1-p)(1-q)$.

questions.text: What is the probability that a divisor of $10^{99}$ is a multiple of $10^{96}$?
questions.subject: 11. Engg. Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: A divisor of $10^{99}=2^{99}5^{99}$ is $2^a5^b$ with $0\le a,b\le99$: 10000 equally likely divisors. Being a multiple of $10^{96}$ requires each exponent in 96,97,98,99: 16 divisors. Probability $16/10000=1/625$.

questions.text:
The degree sequence of a simple graph is the sequence of the degrees of the nodes in the graph in decreasing order. Which of the following sequences can not be the degree sequence of any graph?
I. 7, 6, 5, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1
II. 6, 6, 6, 6, 3, 3, 2, 2
III. 7, 6, 6, 4, 4, 3, 2, 2
IV. 8, 7, 7, 6, 4, 2, 1, 1
questions.subject: 1. Discrete Maths
questions.referenceAnswer: II is not graphical: its first four degrees sum to 24, exceeding the Erdos-Gallai bound $4\cdot3+(3+3+2+2)=22$. IV has degree 8 with only eight vertices, impossible in a simple graph. Havel-Hakimi reduction succeeds for I and III. Thus II and IV only.

questions.text: Suppose the predicate $F(x, y, t)$ is used to represent the statement that person $x$ can fool person $y$ at time $t$. Which one of the statements below expresses best the meaning of the formula $\forall x \exists y \exists t (\neg F(x, y, t))$?

questions.text:
A 5-stage pipelined processor has Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Perform Operation (PO) and Write Operand (WO) stages. The IF, ID, OF and WO stages take 1 clock cycle each for any instruction. The PO stage takes 1 clock cycle for ADD and SUB instructions 3 clock cycles for MUL instruction, and 6 clock cycles for DIV instruction respectively. Operand forwarding is used in the pipeline. What is the number of clock cycles needed to execute the following sequence of instructions?
[CODE]
questions.code:
Instruction          Meaning of Instruction
I0: MUL R2, R0, R1   R2 <- R0 * R1
I1: DIV R5, R3, R4   R5 <- R3/R4
I2: ADD R2, R5, R2   R2 <- R5 + R2
I3: SUB R5, R2, R6   R5 <- R2 - R6

questions.referenceAnswer: The single PO stage executes MUL during cycles 4-6, DIV during 7-12, ADD in 13 and SUB in 14. Forwarding supplies the dependent ADD and SUB operands without waiting for register write-back. The last WO is in cycle 15. This assumes the conventional in-order, non-overlapped PO unit described by the stage model.

questions.text: The weight of a sequence $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1}$ of real numbers is defined as $a_0+\frac{a_1}{2}+\cdots+\frac{a_{n-1}}{2^{n-1}}$. A subsequence of a sequence is obtained by deleting some elements from the sequence, keeping the order of the remaining elements the same. Let $X$ denote the maximum possible weight of a subsequence of $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1}$ and $Y$ the maximum possible weight of a subsequence of $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{n-1}$. Then $X$ is equal to
questions.subject: 7. Algorithms

questions.referenceAnswer: A pushdown automaton can count zeros against ones at ratios 1:1 or 2:1, with a finite-state offset for $i=2j+1$. The unequal cases split into the unions i<j or i>j, and i<2j or i>2j, each checkable by such a PDA. All four languages are context free.

questions.text: Let $w$ be any string of length $n$ in $\{0, 1\}^*$. Let L be the set of all substrings of $w$. What is the minimum number of states in a non-deterministic finite automaton that accepts L?
questions.subject: 2. TOC
questions.referenceAnswer: A path through n+1 states labeled by w, with every state initial-eligible via epsilon transitions from its first state and every state accepting, recognizes all substrings (epsilon included); one can instead add nondeterministic restart transitions from the initial state along matching positions, without adding states. For the lower bound, any accepting path for length-n w must visit n+1 distinct states: a repeated state would permit pumping to accept strings longer than n, impossible for this finite language. Hence n+1.

questions.text:
Consider the following schedule for transactions T1, T2 and T3:
$$\begin{array}{lll}\text{T1}&\text{T2}&\text{T3}\\\text{Read (X)}&&\\&\text{Read (Y)}&\\&&\text{Read (Y)}\\&\text{Write (Y)}&\\\text{Write (X)}&&\\&&\text{Write (X)}\\&\text{Read (X)}&\\&\text{Write (X)}&\\\end{array}$$
Which one of the schedules below is the correct serialization of the above?
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: Conflicts on X give $T_1\to T_3$, $T_1\to T_2$, and $T_3\to T_2$. On Y, T3's read precedes T2's write, also giving $T_3\to T_2$. The only topological order is $T_1,T_3,T_2$.

questions.text:
The following functional dependencies hold for relations $R(A,B,C)$ and $S(B,D,E)$:
$B\to A$
$A\to C$
The relation R contains 200 tuples and the relation S contains 100 tuples. What is the maximum number of tuples possible in the natural join $R\bowtie S$?
questions.subject: 12. DBMS
questions.referenceAnswer: In R, $B\to A\to C$ makes B a key. Each tuple of S can therefore join to at most one R tuple. With all 100 S tuples matching, the maximum is 100, regardless of the 200 tuples in R.

questions.text:
The following program is to be tested for statement coverage: [CODE]
The test cases T1, T2, T3 and T4 given below are expressed in terms of the properties satisfied by the values of variables a, b, c and d. The exact values are not given.
T1 : a, b, c and d are all equal 
T2 : a, b, c and d are all distinct 
T3 : a = b and c != d 
T4 : a !=b and c = d 
Which of the test suites given below ensures coverage of statements S1, S2, S3 and S4?
questions.subject: 8. C Prog
questions.referenceAnswer: T1 takes S1 and exits; T2 takes S3 and exits; T4 takes S2 and then S4. These together cover all four statements. T3 also takes S1, so the other suites each omit at least one branch.

questions.text:
The following program consists of 3 concurrent processes and 3 binary semaphores. The semaphores are initialized as S0 = 1, S1 = 0, S2 = 0.
[CODE]
How many times will process P0 print '0'?
questions.subject: 5. Operating Systems
questions.referenceAnswer: The first print releases S1 and S2. P1 and P2 can each release S0 once, but S0 is binary: if both releases occur before the next wait, they coalesce and the program prints twice total; if P0 consumes between releases, it prints three times. Under the usual eventual-scheduling assumption, at least twice is the guaranteed choice.

notes: Answer transcribed from the printed chapter key, PDF page 5 / book page 551.

questions.text:
A system has n resources $R_0,R_1,\ldots,R_{n-1}$, and k processes $P_0,P_1,\ldots,P_{k-1}$. The implementation of the resource request logic of each process $P_i$, is as follows:
[CODE]
In which one of the following situations is a deadlock possible?
questions.subject: 5. Operating Systems
questions.referenceAnswer: At n=21,k=12, process P10 requests R10 then R12, whereas P9 requests R12 then R10. Each can hold its first resource and wait for the other, forming a deadlock. For even n the even and odd process chains use different resource parity and have no opposing cycle. For n=41,k=19 the increasing even requests and decreasing odd-index-process requests do not overlap to form a cycle.

notes: Answer transcribed from the printed Deadlock key, PDF page 3 / book page 563.

questions.text: Suppose computers A and B have IP addresses 10.105.1.113 and 10.105.1.91 respectively and they both use the same netmask N. Which of the values of N given below should not be used if A and B should belong to the same network?
questions.subject: 3. Computer Networks
questions.referenceAnswer: The final octets are 113=01110001 and 91=01011011. They share their first two bits, so /24, /25 and /26 place them together. With /27 (255.255.255.224), their network octets are 96 and 64, respectively, so they differ.

The memory access times are 2 nanoseconds, 20 nanoseconds and 200 nanoseconds for L1 cache, L2 cache and main memory unit respectively.

When there is a miss in L1 cache and a hit in L2 cache, a block is transferred from L2 cache to L1 cache. What is the time taken for this transfer?
questions.subject: 4. COA

A computer system has an L1 cache, an L2 cache, and a main memory unit connected as shown below. The block size in L1 cache is 4 words. The block size in L2 cache is 16 words. The memory access times are 2 nanoseconds, 20 nanoseconds and 200 nanoseconds for L1 cache, L2 cache and main memory unit respectively.

When there is a miss in both L1 cache and L2 cache, first a block is transferred from main memory to L2 cache, and then a block is transferred from L2 cache to L1 cache. What is the total time taken for these transfers?
questions.subject: 4. COA
questions.referenceAnswer: An L2 block has 16 words and the bus carries four words, requiring four memory-to-L2 transfers. Counting both the source read and destination write gives $4(200+20)=880$ ns. The requested four-word L1 block then costs $20+2=22$ ns, totaling 902 ns, option C. GATE Overflow's worked answer uses this model, but its discussion also notes differing access-time/overlap assumptions and the 968-ns convention. The source does not resolve these assumptions; retain C as a reference and self-assess.

Statement for Linked Answer Questions 54 and 55:
Consider a network with 6 routers R1 to R6 connected with links having weights as shown in the following diagram.
[IMG_1]
All the routers use the distance vector based routing algorithm to update their routing tables. Each router starts with its routing table initialized to contain an entry for each neighbour with the weight of the respective connecting link.
After all the routing tables stabilize, how many links in the network will never be used for carrying any data?
questions.subject: 3. Computer Networks
questions.referenceAnswer: A link is unused if a strictly cheaper alternate path connects its endpoints. R1-R2 costs 6 but R1-R3-R2 costs 3+2=5. R4-R6 costs 8 but R4-R5-R6 costs 1+4=5. All remaining links are themselves shortest endpoint paths. Thus two links are unused.

questions.text: 25 persons are in a room. 15 of them play hockey, 17 of them play football and 10 of them play both hockey and football. Then the number of persons playing neither hockey nor football is:
questions.referenceAnswer: By inclusion-exclusion, $|H\cup F|=15+17-10=22$. Therefore $25-22=3$ people play neither sport.

questions.text:
The question below consists of a pair of related words followed by four pairs of words. Select the pair that best expresses the relation in the original pair:
Unemployed : Worker
questions.referenceAnswer: An unemployed worker is available for work but presently unused; fallow land is cultivable land presently left uncultivated. This is the closest parallel.

The given equality uses base 8: $137_8+276_8=435_8$. In $731_8+672_8$, the units give 3; the next column gives $3+7=10$ decimal, digit 2 with carry 1; the hundreds give $7+6+1=14$ decimal, digit 6 with carry 1. Thus the result is $1623_8$, option C.

questions.text:
Hari (H), Gita (G), Irfan (I) and Saira (S) are siblings (i.e., brothers and sisters). All were born on $1^{\mathrm{st}}$ January. The age difference between any two successive siblings (that is born one after another) is less than 3 years. Given the following facts:
i. Hari's age + Gita's age > Irfan's age + Saira's age.
ii. The age difference between Gita and Saira is 1 year. However, Gita is not the oldest and Saira is not the youngest.
iii. There are no twins.
In what order were they born (oldest first)?
questions.referenceAnswer: All birthdays are the same date and there are no twins, so a one-year difference means G and S are adjacent in birth order. A puts I between S and G and fails. In C and D, I>H and S>G, contradicting H+G>I+S. B is feasible: ages S=4,G=3,H=2,I=0 have successive gaps 1,1,2 and H+G=5>I+S=4. Thus SGHI.

questions.text:
Modern warfare has changed from large scale clashes of armies to suppression of civilian populations. Chemical agents that do their work silently appear to be suited to such warfare; and regretfully, there exist people in military establishments who think that chemical agents are useful tools for their cause.

Which of the following statements best sums up the meaning of the above passage:
questions.optA: Modern warfare has resulted in civil strife.
questions.optB: Chemical agents are useful in modern warfare.
questions.optC: Use of chemical agents in warfare would be undesirable.
questions.optD: People in military establishments like to use chemical agents in war.
questions.referenceAnswer: The accepted GATE Overflow reference chooses D because the passage reports that people in military establishments regard chemical agents as useful. However, 'regretfully' also supports the author's disapproval in C, and D's broad 'like to use' is stronger than 'there exist people ... who think ... useful'. The discussion explicitly contests C versus D (and mentions B). Preserve the literal passage and all choices; use D only as the conventional reference and self-assess this disputed reading item.

questions.text: 5 skilled workers can build a wall in 20 days; 8 semi-skilled workers can build a wall in 25 days; 10 unskilled workers can build a wall in 30 days. If a team has 2 skilled, 6 semi-skilled and 5 unskilled workers, how long will it take to build the wall?
questions.referenceAnswer: A skilled worker builds $1/(5\cdot20)=1/100$ wall per day; a semi-skilled worker 1/200; an unskilled worker 1/300. The team's rate is $2/100+6/200+5/300=1/15$. Therefore it needs 15 days.

questions.text: Given digits 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4 how many distinct 4 digit numbers greater than 3000 can be formed?
questions.referenceAnswer: A four-digit number above 3000 starts with 3 or 4. If it starts with 3, the remaining three places have 27 strings over {2,3,4}, but 222 exceeds the two available 2s and 333 would need four 3s overall: 25 valid. If it starts with 4, only 222 is invalid: 26 valid. Total 25+26=51.
